'''''Angelica sylvestris''''' or '''wild angelica''' is a species of [[flowering plant]], native to Europe and central Asia. An [[annual plant|annual]] or short-lived [[perennial plant|perennial]] growing to a maximum of {{convert|2.5|m|ft|abbr=on}}, it has erect purplish stems and rounded umbels of minuscule white or pale pink flowers in late summer.<ref name= Council>{{cite web |url= http://www.nbisc.ca/species/angelicasylvestris.html |title=Woodland Angelica - Angelica sylvestris |website= nbisc.ca| publisher= New Brunswick Invasive Species Council |access-date=4 August 2011 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110917065915/http://www.nbisc.ca/Species/Angelicasylvestris.html |archive-date=17 September 2011 }}</ref><ref name=AZEGP>{{cite book

==Habitat and ecology==
The Latin [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''sylvestris'' means "growing in woodland",<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for Gardeners |year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |location=UK |isbn=978-1-84533-731-5 }}</ref> but it tolerates a range of conditions, including fields, hedgerows, open woods, marshes, and fens. It grows in light (sandy), medium (loamy), and heavy (clay) soils.

It has recently been determined to be an invasive weed in New Brunswick and Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, Canada. "According to the New Brunswick Invasive Species Council, unless this species is controlled, woodland angelica could spread throughout Canada, overwhelming other vegetation."<ref>{{cite news| url= http://www.natureconservancy.ca/site/News2?page%3DNewsArticle%26id%3D13554%26news_iv_ctrl%3D0%26abbr%3Dat_ncc_ |title=Invasive species going wild in the Saint John River Valley |website= natureconservancy.ca | publisher= |access-date=August 4, 2011 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110927054751/http://www.natureconservancy.ca/site/News2?page=NewsArticle&id=13554&news_iv_ctrl=0&abbr=at_ncc_ |archive-date= September 27, 2011 }}</ref><ref name= Council /> The flowers are visited by a wide array of insects, are thus characterised by a generalised [[pollination]] system.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1111/plb.12328|title=Competition for pollinators and intra-communal spectral dissimilarity of flowers |journal=Plant Biology|year=2015|last1=Van Der Kooi|first1=C. J.|last2=Pen|first2=I.|last3=Staal|first3=M.|last4=Stavenga|first4=D. G.| last5= Elzenga| first5=J. T. M.| display-authors= 3| url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273158762|pmid=25754608|volume=18|issue=1|pages=56–62|hdl=11370/caee8d0d-9724-4056-9d45-93162a5a7afc|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Adult wasps of ''[[Dolichovespula norwegica]]'' are known to feed off the nectar provided by ''A. sylvestris''.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.commanster.eu/commanster/Insects/Bees/SuBees/Dolichovespula.norwegica.html |title=Dolichovespula norwegica |website= commanster.eu |publisher= Ecology of Commanster |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20141006084814/http://www.commanster.eu/commanster/Insects/Bees/SuBees/Dolichovespula.norwegica.html |archive-date=2014-10-06 }}</ref>

==Cultivation and uses==
''A. sylvestris'' is cultivated in gardens. The cultivar 'Ebony', with pink flowers, has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/327488/i-Angelica-sylvestris-i-Ebony/Details |title = Angelica sylvestris 'Ebony' |website= rhs.org.uk | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date=12 January 2018}}</ref>

The vegetable was eaten until the 20th century. The plant can be stored. The stem was eaten fresh, and the leaves could be boiled to a stew for storage or cooked with [[milk]]. The plant has also been used for [[dyeing]].{{citation needed|date=November 2020}}
